record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.context_brief: soft and hard glass DBT framework
record.original_question: Can ductile-to-brittle transitions in soft amorphous materials be described in the same conceptual framework as ductile-to-brittle transitions in hard glasses, while accounting for the dual solid-liquid viscoelastic behavior of soft glasses and the distinction between athermal quasi-static and finite-rate yielding?

evidence.quote: Another key issue is whether the DBT in soft amorphous materials can be described along with that in hard glasses. In particular, soft glassy materials generically show a dual solid–liquid behavior at rest, i.e., viscoelasticity . Therefore, they may display elastic and/or viscous responses depending on the applied strain rate, which strongly impacts the stress response and leads to a key distinction between quasi-static approaches and finite-rate descriptions of yielding.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider amorphous solids subjected to mechanical loading, and the phenomenon of the ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT): under variation of preparation protocol, temperature, or loading rate, the macroscopic yielding response of such materials can change from a smooth, ductile flow to an abrupt, brittle failure characterized by a stress drop and localized shear-band formation. Two broad classes of amorphous solids are distinguished:

(i) Hard glasses (e.g., metallic, oxide, or polymeric glasses), typically modeled as athermal or weakly thermal disordered solids whose yielding under quasi-static shear is described by elasto-plastic models, mean-field depinning-like theories, or random first-order transition theory. For these systems a DBT framework exists in terms of the competition between plastic activity and elastic stress redistribution, with control parameters such as the degree of annealing (initial energy) and the system size.

(ii) Soft amorphous solids (e.g., dense colloidal suspensions, emulsions, foams, gels, microgels), which generically exhibit dual solid–liquid viscoelastic behavior at rest: their mechanical response interpolates between elastic and viscous regimes depending on the applied strain rate \(\dot\gamma\), with a characteristic relaxation time \(\tau\) such that \(\dot\gamma\tau\) is order one in typical experiments. As a consequence, the distinction between athermal quasi-static (AQS) yielding (\(\dot\gamma\tau\to 0\)) and finite-rate yielding (\(\dot\gamma\tau \gtrsim 1\)) is essential.

Formulate a single conceptual and quantitative framework that simultaneously describes the DBT in both classes, in which:

(a) Hard-glass DBT phenomenology is recovered in the limit of negligible viscous dissipation and AQS driving;

(b) The viscoelastic solid–liquid duality of soft glasses is incorporated, e.g., via a constitutive law combining elastic, plastic, and viscous contributions, so that finite strain-rate effects modify the location and sharpness of the transition;

(c) Universal control parameters (such as a dimensionless number combining preparation history, strain rate, and relaxation time) determine on which side of the DBT the system lies, and predict the associated scaling of avalanche statistics, stress overshoot, and shear-band formation.

Prove or disprove that such a unified framework exists, and either construct it explicitly and derive its predictions or identify a rigorous obstruction showing that hard-glass and soft-glass DBT phenomena cannot be subsumed under a single theory.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a conceptual open problem in the rheology and physics of amorphous solids. Recent reviews and research on yielding transitions in soft and hard amorphous materials continue to treat the unification of their DBT descriptions as an open issue, with active work on elasto-plastic and fluidity models incorporating viscoelasticity, but no consensus unified framework has been established.
